idiom_name: extract-method then extract-class: thin adapter + plain collaborator over a service interface
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: identify the element the host calls but a test cannot construct (framework widget, request handler, entry point, active object), apply Extract Method so the decisions sit in one place, then Extract Class - or move them to a plain module - so they live outside the framework-dependent component. The remaining adapter keeps a fixed sequence: read the context, translate it into plain data, delegate to the collaborator, apply the result. Expose the collaborator through a service interface (an interface, trait, function-pointer table or injected function) that tests call directly or replace with a double, and pass the context in as arguments instead of letting the collaborator call back into the host. Keep the humble part small enough to verify by reading, and cover the remaining glue with a few integration checks, since the adapter itself stays outside the unit tests.
code_sketch:
# humble shell (the framework calls this)
def on_event():
    data = read_context()        # framework context -> plain data
    result = decide(data)        # delegate: every decision lives there
    write_back(result)           # plain data -> framework

# the test drives the collaborator directly, without the framework
def test_decide():
    assert decide(sample) == expected
pitfalls: Extracting too little: the shell keeps one branch or validation and the untestable element still owns a decision.
Widening visibility (private to public, test-only flags) instead of extracting, which couples tests to internals.
Letting the collaborator query the host for data, which drags the environment back into the tests.
Verifying delegation with an active mock on the framework's thread, where assertion failures are never observed.

Wrong move: extracting every three-line callback into its own interface-plus-class pair -> the codebase fills with single-caller pass-through layers whose indirection costs more than the risk they remove -> extract only where the environment actually blocks testing and leave pure wiring to a few integration tests.

Wrong move: after extraction, testing only the collaborator and assuming the shell is safe because it is simple -> wiring regressions in the shell (broken binding, forgotten lifecycle forwarding, wrong thread) ship green -> keep a couple of integration or approval tests that drive the real host path.

Wrong move: making the collaborator's internals public so the host's integration tests can read them (a recurring outcome in Unity-style extractions) -> tests pin internals, encapsulation erodes and every refactor breaks tests -> assert through the public interface or inject a minimal, intentional test hook.
sources: Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns (2007), Humble Object
Michael Feathers, The Humble Dialog Box (2002) — https://martinfowler.com/articles/humble-dialog-box.html
Robert C. Martin, Clean Architecture (2017), Chapter 23
